## Harlan, James
**Born:** 1820-08-26 Clark County, Illinois
**Died:** 1899-10-05 Mount Pleasant, Iowa

## Harlan, James
James Harlan was a lawyer, educator, state government official, U.S. senator, secretary of the interior, and father-in-law of Robert T. Lincoln. Harlan lived in Clark County, Illinois, until the age of four, when he moved with his family to Parke County, Indiana. He attended rural schools, helped his father on the family farm, and taught school until 1841, when he entered college. In 1845, he graduated from Asbury (DePauw) University, and that same year he married Ann Eliza Peck, with whom he would have four children. James and Ann moved to Iowa City, Iowa Territory, where he became the leader of Iowa City College. Harlan became interested in local and state politics, and in 1847, he won election, as a Whig, as state superintendent of public instruction. State authorities denied him the office, however, after determining that the election was of dubious legality. Harlan lost in a second election in 1848. Turning to the law, Harlan earned admission to the Iowa bar in 1850 and commenced practicing law in Iowa City. In 1852, he served as deputy surveyor of Wisconsin and Iowa, and the next year, he returned to education, becoming president of Mount Pleasant Collegiate Institute (Iowa Wesleyan University). He remained president of the institute until 1855, when he won election, as a Free Soiler, to the U.S. Senate. Harlan presented his credentials and took his seat in December 1855, but the Iowa Senate declared the seat vacant in January 1857 over election irregularities. Harlan won the special election to fill the vacancy, and in 1860, won reelection, serving in the Senate from January 1857 to May 1865. Harlan gravitated to the Republican Party, and upon commencement of the Civil War, he became a strong proponent of a vigorous prosecution of the war. He supported the confiscation of rebel-owned property and the enlistment of African-Americans in the U.S. Army. He worked to secure passage of the Homestead Act and the Pacific Railroad Act. Harlan also supported President Abraham Lincoln's policy of censoring Democratic newspapers. President Lincoln and Harlan grew closer when Robert T.

## Harlan, James
Lincoln began courting Harlan's daughter Mary, and in March 1865, Lincoln nominated Harlan to become secretary of the interior. The Senate confirmed Harlan's nomination, and he formally took office in May 1865. He remained in the cabinet until June 1866, when he resigned, and returned to the Senate in March 1867, serving until March 1873.

Title: Two Iowans played key roles in the first impeachment of a U.S. president
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
March 4, 2019, 11:39 a.m. CT
The possible impeachment of a president is in the air. For Iowa history fans, this is an occasion to look back to the first impeachment of a U.S. president, when two Iowans played notable roles.
One of the Iowans was a leader in the effort to remove Andrew Johnson from office. The other cast a crucial vote to keep the president in office in one of the most dramatic moments in the history of the U.S. Senate.
The dissenter was U.S. Senator James W. Grimes of Iowa. Grimes was recovering from a stroke that left him partially paralyzed. He arranged to have himself carried onto the Senate floor on the fateful day of the vote. When his name was called, he managed to stand and shout his vote for acquittal.
The motion to convict Johnson and remove him from office fell one vote short of the necessary two-thirds. Grimes was one of seven Republicans who broke with their party in voting to acquit. One of the senators, Edmund Ross of Kansas, was featured by John F. Kennedy in his book “Profiles in Courage.”
It took enormous courage for a Republican to oppose removing the hated President Johnson.
“Never in the political history of the country has there been such a fierce and ungovernable outcry of rage and denunciation raised against public officials as was hurled by the Republican press and people at the seven Republican senators,” wrote Iowa historian Benjamin Gue, who lived through those days. “It drove all of them from public life.”
Grimes endured abuse from Iowans that was “almost unanimous and brutal in the extreme.” Until that vote on May 16, 1868, Grimes was a revered figure in Iowa. As governor in the 1850s, he was a founder of the Republican Party and a staunch proponent of the party’s anti-slavery principles. Now he was a pariah. With his health failing, he resigned from the Senate. He died in his hometown of Burlington in 1872 at age 55.
The other Iowan involved in Johnson’s impeachment was Congressman James F. Wilson of Fairfield in Jefferson County. He was sometimes called “Jefferson Jim” to distinguish him from another prominent Iowa politician of the era, “Tama Jim” Wilson.

Wilson was chairman of the House Judiciary Committee when momentum was building for Johnson’s impeachment. Congress was controlled by so-called Radical Republicans (including the Iowa delegation) who in the aftermath of the Civil War wanted to reconstruct the South to guide freed slaves toward full citizenship. President Johnson opposed the Republicans at every turn, and was an unlikeable fellow besides.
Wilson and his committee spent a year investigating Johnson. In December 1867, a House vote on a resolution to impeach Johnson failed to carry. Wilson spoke in opposition to the resolution.
Wilson said he believed Johnson to the “the worst of the presidents” who displayed “trait of character bad almost beyond precedent.” But he said Johnson should not be impeached because the investigation failed to turn up evidence that he had committed any crime.
Two months later, Feb. 24, 1868, Wilson and the House reversed themselves and approved a resolution of impeachment. Johnson had committed the “crime” of firing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, in violation of the Tenure of Office Act, which required the president to get approval of the Senate before removing any officers.
Wilson declared that impeachment was necessary because Johnson had willfully violated a criminal statute. “He will not obey the law, and by it he must be judged,” declared Wilson.
The House of Representatives appointed a team of prosecutors to present the case for impeachment at a trial in the Senate. Wilson was part of the prosecution team. In the Senate, Grimes cast his dramatic vote to acquit. Iowa’s other senator, James Harlan, voted to convict.
It is sometimes said that Grimes voted to acquit because he disliked Benjamin Wade, president pro tempore of the Senate, who would have become president if Johnson were removed. In a statement, Grimes' arguments were on a higher plane. He argued that Johnson should be given the opportunity to challenge the constitutionality of Tenure of Office Act in court. Grimes saw the act for what it was, an attempt by Congress to subvert the Constitution and make Congress the supreme branch of government.
“This government can only be preserved and the liberty of the people maintained by preserving intact the co-ordinate branches of it — legislative, executive and judicial alike. I am no convert to any doctrine of the omnipotence of Congress.
“I cannot agree to destroy the harmonious working of the Constitution for the sake of getting rid of an unacceptable president.”

_Richard Doak is a former Register opinion editor who retired in early 2007 after a 42-year career at the Register. He currently serves on the Register's editorial board._

# James Harlan (1865–1866)
## James Harlan (1865–1866)
James Harlan was born in Clark County, Illinois, in 1820. He received his education at an Indiana county school and taught in a district school before attending Indiana Asbury University (now DePauw University), graduating in 1845. Later that year, he moved to Iowa City, Iowa, and by 1847 was serving as superintendent of public instruction.
Harlan also studied the law and was admitted to the bar in 1850, the same year he declined the Whig nomination to become governor of Iowa. From 1853 to 1855, Harlan served as president of Iowa Wesleyan College, before being elected to the United States Senate in 1855 as a Free Soiler. Because of irregularities associated with that election, he ran for the Senate yet again in 1857, this time as a Republican -- having joined the newly created party in 1856 -- and successfully defended his seat.
Harlan was reelected again in 1860 but did not serve out his full term, for in 1865 President Abraham Lincoln tapped him to become secretary of the interior following the resignation of John Palmer Usher. Although he had been confirmed, Harlan had not yet taken office when Lincoln was assassinated and therefore could not become secretary of the interior unless President Johnson renominated him. The new President did so, and Harlan assumed his post. However, after a year in office, Harlan resigned in protest over the administration's policies.
Harlan immediately reassumed his old Senate seat but failed to secure reelection in 1872, having been tainted with corruption -- charges that were never proven. Yet the cloud of corruption continued to follow Harlan, preventing yet another successful run for the Senate in 1875. Although renominated yet again in 1881, Harlan withdrew and served as the presiding judge of the Alabama Claims Commission from 1882 to 1886. James Harlan died in 1899.

March 4, 2019, 11:39 a.m. CT
The possible impeachment of a president is in the air. For Iowa history fans, this is an occasion to look back to the first impeachment of a U.S. president, when two Iowans played notable roles.
One of the Iowans was a leader in the effort to remove Andrew Johnson from office. The other cast a crucial vote to keep the president in office in one of the most dramatic moments in the history of the U.S. Senate.
The dissenter was U.S. Senator James W. Grimes of Iowa. Grimes was recovering from a stroke that left him partially paralyzed. He arranged to have himself carried onto the Senate floor on the fateful day of the vote. When his name was called, he managed to stand and shout his vote for acquittal.
The motion to convict Johnson and remove him from office fell one vote short of the necessary two-thirds. Grimes was one of seven Republicans who broke with their party in voting to acquit. One of the senators, Edmund Ross of Kansas, was featured by John F. Kennedy in his book “Profiles in Courage.”
It took enormous courage for a Republican to oppose removing the hated President Johnson.
“Never in the political history of the country has there been such a fierce and ungovernable outcry of rage and denunciation raised against public officials as was hurled by the Republican press and people at the seven Republican senators,” wrote Iowa historian Benjamin Gue, who lived through those days. “It drove all of them from public life.”
Grimes endured abuse from Iowans that was “almost unanimous and brutal in the extreme.” Until that vote on May 16, 1868, Grimes was a revered figure in Iowa. As governor in the 1850s, he was a founder of the Republican Party and a staunch proponent of the party’s anti-slavery principles. Now he was a pariah. With his health failing, he resigned from the Senate. He died in his hometown of Burlington in 1872 at age 55.
The other Iowan involved in Johnson’s impeachment was Congressman James F. Wilson of Fairfield in Jefferson County. He was sometimes called “Jefferson Jim” to distinguish him from another prominent Iowa politician of the era, “Tama Jim” Wilson.
texts.1:
Wilson was chairman of the House Judiciary Committee when momentum was building for Johnson’s impeachment. Congress was controlled by so-called Radical Republicans (including the Iowa delegation) who in the aftermath of the Civil War wanted to reconstruct the South to guide freed slaves toward full citizenship. President Johnson opposed the Republicans at every turn, and was an unlikeable fellow besides.
Wilson and his committee spent a year investigating Johnson. In December 1867, a House vote on a resolution to impeach Johnson failed to carry. Wilson spoke in opposition to the resolution.
Wilson said he believed Johnson to the “the worst of the presidents” who displayed “trait of character bad almost beyond precedent.” But he said Johnson should not be impeached because the investigation failed to turn up evidence that he had committed any crime.
Two months later, Feb. 24, 1868, Wilson and the House reversed themselves and approved a resolution of impeachment. Johnson had committed the “crime” of firing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, in violation of the Tenure of Office Act, which required the president to get approval of the Senate before removing any officers.
Wilson declared that impeachment was necessary because Johnson had willfully violated a criminal statute. “He will not obey the law, and by it he must be judged,” declared Wilson.
The House of Representatives appointed a team of prosecutors to present the case for impeachment at a trial in the Senate. Wilson was part of the prosecution team. In the Senate, Grimes cast his dramatic vote to acquit. Iowa’s other senator, James Harlan, voted to convict.
It is sometimes said that Grimes voted to acquit because he disliked Benjamin Wade, president pro tempore of the Senate, who would have become president if Johnson were removed. In a statement, Grimes' arguments were on a higher plane. He argued that Johnson should be given the opportunity to challenge the constitutionality of Tenure of Office Act in court. Grimes saw the act for what it was, an attempt by Congress to subvert the Constitution and make Congress the supreme branch of government.
“This government can only be preserved and the liberty of the people maintained by preserving intact the co-ordinate branches of it — legislative, executive and judicial alike. I am no convert to any doctrine of the omnipotence of Congress.
“I cannot agree to destroy the harmonious working of the Constitution for the sake of getting rid of an unacceptable president.”

**James Harlan** (August 26, 1820 – October 5, 1899) was an attorney and politician, a member of the United States Senate, a U.S. Cabinet Secretary at the United States Department of Interior under President Andrew Johnson, and a Federal Judge.
texts.1:
Harlan was born on August 26, 1820, in Clark County, Illinois, and raised in Indiana. He was the son of Silas Harlan (1792–1868) and Mary (née Connolly) Harlan (1796–1896).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-Brigham1918-1)
As a boy, Harlan attended local schools before graduating from Indiana Asbury University (now DePauw University) in 1845.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-JHbioguide-2)
In 1845, he moved to Iowa City, Iowa, where he served as Superintendent of Schools. He also studied law and was admitted to the bar in 1850.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-JHbioguide-2) He joined the Whig Party and became active in politics. In 1850, Harlan declined the Whig nomination for Governor of Iowa. From 1853 to 1855, Harlan was president of Iowa Wesleyan College in Mount Pleasant, Iowa.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-JHbioguide-2)
texts.2:
### First Senate tenure
[edit]
Hon. James Harlan
In 1855, Harlan was elected by the Iowa legislature to the United States Senate as a Free Soil Party candidate. In 1857, the U.S. Senate declared the seat vacant because of irregularities in that legislative election. He was re-elected by the legislature and seated as a Republican, serving until 1865. In 1861, Harlan was a Delegate to the Peace Conference that tried to arrange a compromise to prevent the American Civil War.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-JHbioguide-2)
texts.3:
### Secretary of the Interior
[edit]
Harlan was a close friend of President Abraham Lincoln and his family. In 1865, after Lincoln's assassination, he resigned from the Senate when he was appointed as Secretary of the Interior under PresidentAndrew Johnson, an appointment he held until 1866. As secretary he announced that he intended to "clean house" and fired "a considerable number of incumbents who were seldom at their respective desks".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-Loving291-3) He had done so after requesting, in late May 1865, a report listing all employees who (1.) uttered disloyal statements since the bombardment of Fort Sumter, (2.) all those not known to entertain loyal sentiments or who had associated with those known to be disloyal, (3.) those who were inefficient or not necessary to transact public business, (4.) all such persons "as disregard in their conduct, habits, and associations, the rules of decorum, [and] propriety proscribed by a christian civilization."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-4)
texts.4:
### Secretary of the Interior
Among this group was the poet Walt Whitman, then working as a clerk in the department, who received his dismissal note on June 30, 1865.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-5) Harlan had found a copy of _Leaves of Grass_ on Whitman's desk as the poet was making revisions and found it to be morally offensive. "I will not have the author of that book in this Department", he said. "If the President of the United States should order his reinstatement, I would resign sooner than I would put him back."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-6) Twenty-nine years later, Harlan defended his firing of Whitman, saying that the clerk was dismissed solely "on the grounds that his services were not needed".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-Loving291-3)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-7)
Harlan was a member of the Southern Treaty Commission that renegotiated treaties with Indian Tribes that had sided with the Confederacy, such as the Cherokee and Choctaw. As part of the new treaties, they had to emancipate their slaves, as was being done by amendment within the United States, and offer them full citizenship in the tribes if they chose to stay in Indian Territory. If they left, the freedmen would become United States citizens. (Membership issues related to the Cherokee Freedmen and Choctaw Freedmen have become significant since the late 20th century.) Harlan resigned from the post in 1866 when he no longer supported the policies of President Johnson.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-Brigham1918-1)

## Harlan, James
**Born:** 1820-08-26 Clark County, Illinois
**Died:** 1899-10-05 Mount Pleasant, Iowa
texts.1:
## Harlan, James
James Harlan was a lawyer, educator, state government official, U.S. senator, secretary of the interior, and father-in-law of Robert T. Lincoln. Harlan lived in Clark County, Illinois, until the age of four, when he moved with his family to Parke County, Indiana. He attended rural schools, helped his father on the family farm, and taught school until 1841, when he entered college. In 1845, he graduated from Asbury (DePauw) University, and that same year he married Ann Eliza Peck, with whom he would have four children. James and Ann moved to Iowa City, Iowa Territory, where he became the leader of Iowa City College. Harlan became interested in local and state politics, and in 1847, he won election, as a Whig, as state superintendent of public instruction. State authorities denied him the office, however, after determining that the election was of dubious legality. Harlan lost in a second election in 1848. Turning to the law, Harlan earned admission to the Iowa bar in 1850 and commenced practicing law in Iowa City. In 1852, he served as deputy surveyor of Wisconsin and Iowa, and the next year, he returned to education, becoming president of Mount Pleasant Collegiate Institute (Iowa Wesleyan University). He remained president of the institute until 1855, when he won election, as a Free Soiler, to the U.S. Senate. Harlan presented his credentials and took his seat in December 1855, but the Iowa Senate declared the seat vacant in January 1857 over election irregularities. Harlan won the special election to fill the vacancy, and in 1860, won reelection, serving in the Senate from January 1857 to May 1865. Harlan gravitated to the Republican Party, and upon commencement of the Civil War, he became a strong proponent of a vigorous prosecution of the war. He supported the confiscation of rebel-owned property and the enlistment of African-Americans in the U.S. Army. He worked to secure passage of the Homestead Act and the Pacific Railroad Act. Harlan also supported President Abraham Lincoln's policy of censoring Democratic newspapers. President Lincoln and Harlan grew closer when Robert T.
texts.2:
## Harlan, James
Lincoln began courting Harlan's daughter Mary, and in March 1865, Lincoln nominated Harlan to become secretary of the interior. The Senate confirmed Harlan's nomination, and he formally took office in May 1865. He remained in the cabinet until June 1866, when he resigned, and returned to the Senate in March 1867, serving until March 1873.

Title: Two Iowans played key roles in the first impeachment of a U.S. president
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
March 4, 2019, 11:39 a.m. CT
The possible impeachment of a president is in the air. For Iowa history fans, this is an occasion to look back to the first impeachment of a U.S. president, when two Iowans played notable roles.
One of the Iowans was a leader in the effort to remove Andrew Johnson from office. The other cast a crucial vote to keep the president in office in one of the most dramatic moments in the history of the U.S. Senate.
The dissenter was U.S. Senator James W. Grimes of Iowa. Grimes was recovering from a stroke that left him partially paralyzed. He arranged to have himself carried onto the Senate floor on the fateful day of the vote. When his name was called, he managed to stand and shout his vote for acquittal.
The motion to convict Johnson and remove him from office fell one vote short of the necessary two-thirds. Grimes was one of seven Republicans who broke with their party in voting to acquit. One of the senators, Edmund Ross of Kansas, was featured by John F. Kennedy in his book “Profiles in Courage.”
It took enormous courage for a Republican to oppose removing the hated President Johnson.
“Never in the political history of the country has there been such a fierce and ungovernable outcry of rage and denunciation raised against public officials as was hurled by the Republican press and people at the seven Republican senators,” wrote Iowa historian Benjamin Gue, who lived through those days. “It drove all of them from public life.”
Grimes endured abuse from Iowans that was “almost unanimous and brutal in the extreme.” Until that vote on May 16, 1868, Grimes was a revered figure in Iowa. As governor in the 1850s, he was a founder of the Republican Party and a staunch proponent of the party’s anti-slavery principles. Now he was a pariah. With his health failing, he resigned from the Senate. He died in his hometown of Burlington in 1872 at age 55.
The other Iowan involved in Johnson’s impeachment was Congressman James F. Wilson of Fairfield in Jefferson County. He was sometimes called “Jefferson Jim” to distinguish him from another prominent Iowa politician of the era, “Tama Jim” Wilson.

Wilson was chairman of the House Judiciary Committee when momentum was building for Johnson’s impeachment. Congress was controlled by so-called Radical Republicans (including the Iowa delegation) who in the aftermath of the Civil War wanted to reconstruct the South to guide freed slaves toward full citizenship. President Johnson opposed the Republicans at every turn, and was an unlikeable fellow besides.
Wilson and his committee spent a year investigating Johnson. In December 1867, a House vote on a resolution to impeach Johnson failed to carry. Wilson spoke in opposition to the resolution.
Wilson said he believed Johnson to the “the worst of the presidents” who displayed “trait of character bad almost beyond precedent.” But he said Johnson should not be impeached because the investigation failed to turn up evidence that he had committed any crime.
Two months later, Feb. 24, 1868, Wilson and the House reversed themselves and approved a resolution of impeachment. Johnson had committed the “crime” of firing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, in violation of the Tenure of Office Act, which required the president to get approval of the Senate before removing any officers.
Wilson declared that impeachment was necessary because Johnson had willfully violated a criminal statute. “He will not obey the law, and by it he must be judged,” declared Wilson.
The House of Representatives appointed a team of prosecutors to present the case for impeachment at a trial in the Senate. Wilson was part of the prosecution team. In the Senate, Grimes cast his dramatic vote to acquit. Iowa’s other senator, James Harlan, voted to convict.
It is sometimes said that Grimes voted to acquit because he disliked Benjamin Wade, president pro tempore of the Senate, who would have become president if Johnson were removed. In a statement, Grimes' arguments were on a higher plane. He argued that Johnson should be given the opportunity to challenge the constitutionality of Tenure of Office Act in court. Grimes saw the act for what it was, an attempt by Congress to subvert the Constitution and make Congress the supreme branch of government.
“This government can only be preserved and the liberty of the people maintained by preserving intact the co-ordinate branches of it — legislative, executive and judicial alike. I am no convert to any doctrine of the omnipotence of Congress.
“I cannot agree to destroy the harmonious working of the Constitution for the sake of getting rid of an unacceptable president.”

_Richard Doak is a former Register opinion editor who retired in early 2007 after a 42-year career at the Register. He currently serves on the Register's editorial board._

**James Harlan** (August 26, 1820 – October 5, 1899) was an attorney and politician, a member of the United States Senate, a U.S. Cabinet Secretary at the United States Department of Interior under President Andrew Johnson, and a Federal Judge.

Harlan was born on August 26, 1820, in Clark County, Illinois, and raised in Indiana. He was the son of Silas Harlan (1792–1868) and Mary (née Connolly) Harlan (1796–1896).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-Brigham1918-1)
As a boy, Harlan attended local schools before graduating from Indiana Asbury University (now DePauw University) in 1845.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-JHbioguide-2)
In 1845, he moved to Iowa City, Iowa, where he served as Superintendent of Schools. He also studied law and was admitted to the bar in 1850.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-JHbioguide-2) He joined the Whig Party and became active in politics. In 1850, Harlan declined the Whig nomination for Governor of Iowa. From 1853 to 1855, Harlan was president of Iowa Wesleyan College in Mount Pleasant, Iowa.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-JHbioguide-2)

### First Senate tenure
[edit]
Hon. James Harlan
In 1855, Harlan was elected by the Iowa legislature to the United States Senate as a Free Soil Party candidate. In 1857, the U.S. Senate declared the seat vacant because of irregularities in that legislative election. He was re-elected by the legislature and seated as a Republican, serving until 1865. In 1861, Harlan was a Delegate to the Peace Conference that tried to arrange a compromise to prevent the American Civil War.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-JHbioguide-2)

### Secretary of the Interior
[edit]
Harlan was a close friend of President Abraham Lincoln and his family. In 1865, after Lincoln's assassination, he resigned from the Senate when he was appointed as Secretary of the Interior under PresidentAndrew Johnson, an appointment he held until 1866. As secretary he announced that he intended to "clean house" and fired "a considerable number of incumbents who were seldom at their respective desks".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-Loving291-3) He had done so after requesting, in late May 1865, a report listing all employees who (1.) uttered disloyal statements since the bombardment of Fort Sumter, (2.) all those not known to entertain loyal sentiments or who had associated with those known to be disloyal, (3.) those who were inefficient or not necessary to transact public business, (4.) all such persons "as disregard in their conduct, habits, and associations, the rules of decorum, [and] propriety proscribed by a christian civilization."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-4)

### Secretary of the Interior
Among this group was the poet Walt Whitman, then working as a clerk in the department, who received his dismissal note on June 30, 1865.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-5) Harlan had found a copy of _Leaves of Grass_ on Whitman's desk as the poet was making revisions and found it to be morally offensive. "I will not have the author of that book in this Department", he said. "If the President of the United States should order his reinstatement, I would resign sooner than I would put him back."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-6) Twenty-nine years later, Harlan defended his firing of Whitman, saying that the clerk was dismissed solely "on the grounds that his services were not needed".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-Loving291-3)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-7)
Harlan was a member of the Southern Treaty Commission that renegotiated treaties with Indian Tribes that had sided with the Confederacy, such as the Cherokee and Choctaw. As part of the new treaties, they had to emancipate their slaves, as was being done by amendment within the United States, and offer them full citizenship in the tribes if they chose to stay in Indian Territory. If they left, the freedmen would become United States citizens. (Membership issues related to the Cherokee Freedmen and Choctaw Freedmen have become significant since the late 20th century.) Harlan resigned from the post in 1866 when he no longer supported the policies of President Johnson.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Harlan_(Iowa_politician)#cite_note-Brigham1918-1)

**Born:** 1820-08-26 Clark County, Illinois
**Died:** 1899-10-05 Mount Pleasant, Iowa

## Harlan, James
James Harlan was a lawyer, educator, state government official, U.S. senator, secretary of the interior, and father-in-law of Robert T. Lincoln. Harlan lived in Clark County, Illinois, until the age of four, when he moved with his family to Parke County, Indiana. He attended rural schools, helped his father on the family farm, and taught school until 1841, when he entered college. In 1845, he graduated from Asbury (DePauw) University, and that same year he married Ann Eliza Peck, with whom he would have four children. James and Ann moved to Iowa City, Iowa Territory, where he became the leader of Iowa City College. Harlan became interested in local and state politics, and in 1847, he won election, as a Whig, as state superintendent of public instruction. State authorities denied him the office, however, after determining that the election was of dubious legality. Harlan lost in a second election in 1848. Turning to the law, Harlan earned admission to the Iowa bar in 1850 and commenced practicing law in Iowa City. In 1852, he served as deputy surveyor of Wisconsin and Iowa, and the next year, he returned to education, becoming president of Mount Pleasant Collegiate Institute (Iowa Wesleyan University). He remained president of the institute until 1855, when he won election, as a Free Soiler, to the U.S. Senate. Harlan presented his credentials and took his seat in December 1855, but the Iowa Senate declared the seat vacant in January 1857 over election irregularities. Harlan won the special election to fill the vacancy, and in 1860, won reelection, serving in the Senate from January 1857 to May 1865. Harlan gravitated to the Republican Party, and upon commencement of the Civil War, he became a strong proponent of a vigorous prosecution of the war. He supported the confiscation of rebel-owned property and the enlistment of African-Americans in the U.S. Army. He worked to secure passage of the Homestead Act and the Pacific Railroad Act. Harlan also supported President Abraham Lincoln's policy of censoring Democratic newspapers. President Lincoln and Harlan grew closer when Robert T.

## Harlan, James
Lincoln began courting Harlan's daughter Mary, and in March 1865, Lincoln nominated Harlan to become secretary of the interior. The Senate confirmed Harlan's nomination, and he formally took office in May 1865. He remained in the cabinet until June 1866, when he resigned, and returned to the Senate in March 1867, serving until March 1873.

# James Harlan (1865–1866)
## James Harlan (1865–1866)
James Harlan was born in Clark County, Illinois, in 1820. He received his education at an Indiana county school and taught in a district school before attending Indiana Asbury University (now DePauw University), graduating in 1845. Later that year, he moved to Iowa City, Iowa, and by 1847 was serving as superintendent of public instruction.
Harlan also studied the law and was admitted to the bar in 1850, the same year he declined the Whig nomination to become governor of Iowa. From 1853 to 1855, Harlan served as president of Iowa Wesleyan College, before being elected to the United States Senate in 1855 as a Free Soiler. Because of irregularities associated with that election, he ran for the Senate yet again in 1857, this time as a Republican -- having joined the newly created party in 1856 -- and successfully defended his seat.
Harlan was reelected again in 1860 but did not serve out his full term, for in 1865 President Abraham Lincoln tapped him to become secretary of the interior following the resignation of John Palmer Usher. Although he had been confirmed, Harlan had not yet taken office when Lincoln was assassinated and therefore could not become secretary of the interior unless President Johnson renominated him. The new President did so, and Harlan assumed his post. However, after a year in office, Harlan resigned in protest over the administration's policies.
Harlan immediately reassumed his old Senate seat but failed to secure reelection in 1872, having been tainted with corruption -- charges that were never proven. Yet the cloud of corruption continued to follow Harlan, preventing yet another successful run for the Senate in 1875. Although renominated yet again in 1881, Harlan withdrew and served as the presiding judge of the Alabama Claims Commission from 1882 to 1886. James Harlan died in 1899.

Based on my research, I can now answer your question.

**The political parties:**
- **William M. Stewart** (Senator from Nevada) 
- **James Harlan** (Senator from Iowa) - Note: The source documents mention this as the Iowa senator who voted for conviction during the Johnson impeachment trial

Both Stewart and Harlan were members of the **Republican Party**.

**The body with Standing Rules derived from Article One:**
This refers to the **U.S. Senate**, which operates under Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution ("Each House shall be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members") and has its own standing rules that differ from those of the House of Representatives.

**When Republicans took control:**
The Republican Party took control of the U.S. Senate in **March 1867**.

James Harlan had served in the Senate from 1857-1865, then became Secretary of the Interior under President Abraham Lincoln in 1865. After resigning from that cabinet post in 1866 due to policy disagreements with President Andrew Johnson regarding Reconstruction, Harlan returned to the Senate in March 1867. His return gave the Republican Party enough seats to establish a working majority in the Senate (the records show 42 Republicans and 12 Democrats serving at the time of the Johnson impeachment trial in March 1868).

Both Stewart and Harlan participated in the historic 1868 impeachment trial of President Andrew Johnson. While Stewart voted along party lines to convict Johnson, Harlan also voted for conviction. However, Johnson was ultimately acquitted by a single vote (35 guilty to 19 not guilty) on May 16, 1868—a vote so close that the impeachment of a sitting President remains one of the closest votes in Senate history.
